name: Cloud Computing Infrastructure
description: Cloud computing infrastructure combines physical computing resources with software that makes them available as configurable services. Iranian provider documentation illustrates this model through virtual servers, resource controls, and consumption-based billing, although advertised capabilities do not establish measured performance.

seo.title: Cloud Computing Infrastructure in Iran | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: Understand cloud infrastructure, virtual servers, customer responsibilities, and the limits of available evidence about Iranian services.

content.heading: What makes infrastructure a cloud?
content.content:
Cloud infrastructure has both a physical foundation and a software layer. Servers, storage equipment, and networks supply the underlying capacity; software organizes that capacity into services customers can provision and manage. The National Institute of Standards and Technology, a United States standards agency commonly abbreviated as NIST, distinguishes cloud computing through self-service, network access, pooled resources, elasticity, and measured use. These characteristics provide a useful vocabulary for examining services in Iran without treating every remotely hosted server as equivalent. [s1]

Infrastructure as a Service, or IaaS, gives customers computing resources on which they can install operating systems and applications. The provider operates the underlying infrastructure, while the customer retains responsibility for the software environment described by that service model. Renting infrastructure therefore changes the division of work; it does not remove the need to administer an application. [s1]

content.heading: How Iranian providers describe the service
content.content:
ParsPack describes its cloud server as a virtualized service drawing processor, memory, and storage resources from physical servers. Its product page says customers can increase or decrease resources and pay according to consumption. The ordering interface separates resource choices from location and operating-system choices, illustrating that a cloud server is a configurable service rather than simply a fixed computer rental. These are provider descriptions, not independently measured findings. [s2]

ArvanCloud's Persian product page likewise advertises configurable virtual servers. It identifies a graphical management interface, an application programming interface, or API, and Terraform, a tool used to describe infrastructure through configuration files. These access methods matter because they offer different ways to manage the same service: an operator can use a control panel, while software can request infrastructure through an interface. The page also describes consumption-based charging. This evidence establishes the advertised product design, but it does not verify provisioning speed, uninterrupted resizing, or billing accuracy. [s3]

content.heading: The questions behind a deployment
content.content:
For an international reader, the useful distinction is between a service being offered and a workload being demonstrably supported. A product description can explain available controls; it cannot establish application reliability under a particular traffic pattern. NIST's public-cloud security guidance treats moving data, applications, and infrastructure outside an organization as a security and privacy decision requiring explicit consideration. That general framework is relevant here, but it is not a statement of Iranian law. [s4]

An evidence-based account of a particular Iranian deployment would therefore need more than a list of server sizes. It would need the applicable service agreement, a clear allocation of operational responsibilities, and records supporting any performance claims. This page provides the technical foundation and documented product examples; the inspected evidence does not support a national capacity estimate or a ranking of providers. [s1][s2][s3][s4]

name: Cloud Storage
description: Cloud storage makes data available through a remotely managed service, with object storage providing a documented example in Iran. Understanding objects, access permissions, versioning, and delivery integration helps distinguish storage features from evidence of recoverability or service performance.

seo.title: Cloud Storage in Iran | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: Explore object storage, permissions, versioning, and documented Iranian storage offerings, with clear limits on performance claims.

content.heading: From files to objects
content.content:
Object storage is a useful starting point for understanding cloud storage. Amazon's documentation describes an object as a file together with metadata describing it, held inside a container called a bucket. A key identifies an object within that bucket. This terminology explains a widely encountered storage model; Amazon's documentation is used here for technical context, not as evidence that its services are available to customers in Iran. [s1]

The distinction matters when reading Iranian product descriptions. ArvanCloud's object-storage page presents storage for website content, images, service media, logs, and backup files. It describes access through the web or an API, meaning an application programming interface through which software can manage data. These examples show how storage can serve an application directly rather than functioning only as a personal folder for uploaded documents. They remain statements about the provider's offering. [s2]

content.heading: Keeping data and controlling access
content.content:
Versioning retains different versions of an object instead of treating every replacement as the only surviving copy. Amazon documents this as a way to restore objects accidentally overwritten or deleted. Its documentation also separates storing an object from granting access to it: permissions determine who may use the stored resource. These are distinct questions, and understanding both is essential to interpreting a storage service. [s1]

ArvanCloud advertises versioning, lifecycle rules for removing objects, and client-side or server-side encryption. Its page also describes storing data in other data centers and integrating buckets with content delivery settings. These features concern different parts of data management: retaining earlier states, controlling retention, protecting stored information, and making content accessible. The inspected material does not demonstrate how these features performed in a recovery exercise or establish that every advertised option was available under every plan. [s2]

content.heading: What the storage promise does not establish
content.content:
A storage feature list is not sufficient evidence of an organization's ability to recover its information. NIST's public-cloud guidance identifies security and privacy challenges when data and services move outside an organization's own environment. Applied to storage, that framing makes the boundary between the customer and provider a central part of the subject: the location of the service, access arrangements, and documented responsibilities all require examination. This is an editorial application of the guidance, not a legal conclusion about Iran. [s3]

For this page, the most defensible conclusion is limited but useful. Public documentation demonstrates that an Iranian provider markets programmable object storage with data-management and delivery features. It does not establish national storage capacity, independently measured durability, or a complete history of service availability. A fuller account needs dated documentation and operational evidence, particularly before presenting advertised resilience as an observed outcome. [s2][s3]

name: CDN Services
description: A content delivery network distributes web content through servers that can reuse cached responses closer to users. Iranian providers market CDN services alongside security and traffic-management features, but product claims alone do not establish nationwide coverage or measured improvements.

seo.title: CDN Services in Iran | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: How content delivery networks work, what Iranian providers advertise, and why caching rules and measured performance matter.

content.heading: Bringing content closer to readers
content.content:
A content delivery network, usually shortened to CDN, uses geographically distributed servers to deliver web content. Cloudflare's technical explanation describes caching content near end users and distinguishes the CDN from the web host that supplies the original content. Images, stylesheets, scripts, and other website assets can be delivered through this intermediate network. A CDN therefore adds a delivery layer to a website rather than automatically replacing its underlying application or hosting service. [s1]

The original source of content is called the origin. An edge server is part of the delivery network that handles requests nearer to users. Reusing an eligible cached response can reduce repeated trips to the origin, but the benefit depends on whether the requested content can actually be reused. This distinction connects the physical distribution of servers with the rules governing the responses they deliver. [s1][s2]

content.heading: Caching is a controlled process
content.content:
The Internet Engineering Task Force's HTTP caching standard distinguishes shared caches, which can serve multiple users, from private caches dedicated to one user. Reuse depends on conditions including the request, relevant headers, freshness, and validation. A response that is fresh can sometimes be reused without checking the origin again; another response may require validation first. [s2]

These distinctions matter for websites that mix public material with personalized pages. The standard defines directives governing storage and reuse, including restrictions associated with private responses and sensitive information. A CDN's ability to cache content is consequently not a reason to treat every response alike. Correct behavior depends on the response rules and the cache configuration, not simply on enabling a delivery service. [s2]

content.heading: What Iranian product pages document
content.content:
ArvanCloud's Persian CDN page advertises content caching, file and image optimization, domain-name management, traffic reporting, and security controls. These controls include rate limiting, which restricts request volume, and a web application firewall, or WAF, intended to identify and block unwanted web requests. The page establishes the advertised range of functions; it does not independently demonstrate protection against every attack or a particular improvement in loading speed. [s3]

ParsPack also markets a CDN with caching, compression, domain-name management, firewall rules, and reporting. Its page contains differing statements about the geographic extent of its network, making a precise coverage count unsuitable for repetition without clarification. More broadly, the presence of similar feature names across providers does not establish equivalent configuration options or outcomes. [s4]

content.title: A simplified cached-content request
content.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A["Reader requests content"] --> B["CDN evaluates request and cached response"]
  B -->|"Reuse is permitted"| C["Return cached response"]
  B -->|"Origin contact is required"| D["Contact origin server"]
  D --> E["Apply response and caching rules"]
  E --> F["Return response to reader"]
```
content.summary: The arrows describe request processing, not ownership or legal authority. The simplified flow omits errors and detailed validation exchanges; a cached response is reused only when applicable rules permit it.

content.heading: Reading performance claims
content.content: For readers comparing Iranian services, the practical question is how a delivery network performs for the intended audience and content. The inspected product pages are evidence of marketed capabilities, while the technical sources explain why caching can help. Neither combination supplies an independent comparison across Iranian networks, locations, or applications. This page therefore avoids provider rankings and treats coverage and speed claims as matters requiring separate measurement. [s1][s3][s4]
